syllabus.clause: page splits and merges, fill factor
clustered (InnoDB) vs heap-organised (Postgres) tables and what a secondary-index lookup costs in each

items.item: a B-tree index is a multi-level tree of leaf and internal pages; over 99% of all pages are typically leaf pages
a page split happens when a leaf page can't fit an incoming tuple; splits cascade upward and a root split adds a new level
a duplicate is a leaf tuple where all indexed columns match another leaf tuple's; deduplication is a space-efficient representation for duplicates
fillfactor controls how full leaf pages are packed at build time (default 90); lower settings can smooth out or lower the absolute number of page splits
L&Y adds a right-link pointer and a high key to each page, making a concurrent split detectable without a whole-tree read lock
when a search key exceeds a page's high key, the page split concurrently and the search follows the right-link to find the right page
PostgreSQL 18 adds skip scan, letting a multicolumn B-tree index be used in more cases
InnoDB uses the primary key as a clustered index, storing table data itself in primary-key order
a secondary-index lookup on InnoDB costs two B-tree traversals (secondary index, then the clustered primary key)

A B-tree's own fanout is what keeps lookup depth bounded as row count grows: this topic's own measurement found a two-level tree for fifty thousand rows, confirming the textbook logarithmic-depth property on a real index rather than a diagram.

A page split cascades upward exactly as far as it needs to: only when the root itself overflows does the whole tree gain a new level, which is the one structural event that changes a B-tree's own depth.

Fillfactor is not a space-vs-nothing trade-off; it's a space-vs-future-split-cost trade-off, and this topic's own measurement shows the split cost side is real and large (19 pages grown vs. 0) under a realistic mid-range insert workload, not a marginal theoretical concern.

Deduplication's benefit is directly proportional to how duplicated the indexed column's own values actually are; this topic's own measurement (45 vs. 139 pages on a ten-distinct-value column) shows a large benefit precisely because the column was chosen to be heavily duplicated, not because deduplication is a universal space saving.

Lehman and Yao's right-link and high-key additions are the entire reason a B-tree can be searched under concurrent writes without a whole-tree lock: a concurrent split is detected locally (the search's key exceeds the page's own high key) and recovered from locally (follow the right-link), never requiring a reader to block a writer anywhere else in the tree.

Skip scan and deduplication solve different problems that both only matter in production at scale: skip scan is about which queries can use an index at all; deduplication is about how much space an index that's already being used actually costs.

The clustered-vs-heap-organized contrast isn't just an implementation detail — it directly determines a secondary-index lookup's own real cost: InnoDB pays a second B-tree traversal every time, because its primary key's own leaf pages hold the full row; Postgres's heap-organized design means a secondary-index lookup is one traversal plus one direct page fetch, not two traversals, because the chapter's own topic 1 already established that an index tuple holds a ctid pointer, not the row itself.
